studies.title: Settle What Is Between You
studies.meaning: A question about property is answered by lifting the property out of the argument. The bounties are declared to belong to God and the Messenger, which does not so much decide who receives what as dissolve the standing of the claims being pressed. Three instructions follow at once, and only the last concerns obedience. The first two are about the questioners themselves: be mindful of God, and repair what has gone wrong between you. The quarrel is treated as the graver problem.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, opening a surah that runs through the encounter at Badr and its aftermath. The classical sources report that the men disagreed after the fighting over what had been gathered. Those who chased the retreating force, those who had stood guard, and those who fought in the line each argued a claim. The early scholars name that dispute as the occasion of the ayah. Several early collections carry the report.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning something given over and above what is owed, the same root behind the word for a voluntary extra prayer. The name itself concedes that nothing here was anyone's due.
The verb for mending what has broken and making something sound again. It is used both of reconciling people and of reforming conduct, so a quarrel is described here in the vocabulary of repair work.
The Arabic idiom treats the space between people as a thing that can be in good or bad condition. What the ayah asks to be put right is not the men themselves but the relation running between them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A raiding party in Arabia divided what it took by a customary reckoning. Everyone knew it and nobody had written it down. Arguments over shares were a standing cause of feud between allied clans. Men who fought side by side in the morning could be enemies by nightfall. One camel was enough. The community at Medina had been put together from tribes recently at war with each other.
studies.didYouKnow: The word this surah is named after occurs only in this one ayah. It appears twice there and nowhere else in the Quran. Its root is the same one behind the word for a voluntary prayer, offered beyond what is prescribed. That is why translators reach for words like bounty, addition or windfall rather than payment.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage puts a question about ownership below a question about relationships. Assigning the property upward takes the dispute out of the terms it was argued in. Nobody can press a claim against God. The ayah then sets one thing beside another. Repairing what is between people sits right next to mindfulness of God. The two are treated as one instruction, not as a duty and a courtesy.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same verb for repairing what is between people, and turns it into a standing rule.
Returns to the same property later in the surah and sets out how a portion of it is assigned.
Names reconciliation between people as one of the few things worth speaking privately to arrange.

studies.applyIt: There is a relationship of yours with a small unrepaired thing in it, probably about something owed or something assumed. Do not wait until you can prove you were right. Send the first message this week, and let it be about the relation rather than the item. The ayah puts the repair before the settlement, deliberately.
studies.explainEasier: People asked about the things taken after the battle. The answer was that they belong to God and his Messenger. The verse then tells them to fix what has gone wrong between them, and to obey God.

studies.title: Hearts That Tremble
studies.meaning: A definition is offered with a restrictive particle. So what follows is presented as what believers are, not as one description among several. Three marks are given, and all three are responses rather than actions. The heart moves when God is mentioned. Faith increases when the verses are recited. Reliance rests on the Lord. Early scholars note that the first two are involuntary, which makes them a test of a person rather than an instruction to them.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. It opens a surah that deals with the battle of Badr and the disagreement over its spoils that followed. The first verse reports that dispute. This description of believers arrives immediately afterwards, before anything is decided. Early scholars read the placement as deliberate. A definition of faith is set down before the community's quarrel about property is addressed at all.

keyTerms.note: A verb for fear that moves the body, distinct from the general word for being afraid. It names the physical flinch rather than the attitude, which is why the heart is given as its subject.
The passive of the verb behind remembrance. The trigger is described as the bare mention of God, not a sermon or an argument, so the response is to a name rather than to a case being made.
From the root for appointing an agent to handle your affairs. It stands in the ongoing present, so reliance is described as a continuous relation rather than as a decision taken once.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Badr had just been fought and won, against odds nobody had expected to survive. The community was now arguing over camels, weapons and captives. The men who had stood in that line were sitting in Medina dividing property. That is the setting into which a description of trembling hearts and reliance is placed. Everyone hearing it had been part of both scenes.
studies.didYouKnow: The surah opens with a question about the spoils of war and answers it in a single line. Then it turns at once to this description of believers, before going back to the battle. Classical scholars note the structure. An argument about property is interrupted by a definition of faith, and the interruption is where the answer actually lies.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Faith is described by what happens to a person rather than by what they profess. So it is something they can observe in themselves without being able to manufacture it. The second mark adds a further claim. The same text produces increase in some listeners and nothing in others. So the response tells you about the hearer rather than about the words. Reliance then turns inward experience outward, into how a person lives.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same trembling of hearts at God's mention, adding patience and prayer.
Says the same recitation increases some in faith while others ask which of them it added to.
Describes skins shivering at the recitation before softening to the remembrance of God.

studies.applyIt: Read or listen to a short passage you already know well. Afterwards ask one honest question: did anything move. Do not manufacture a feeling. The verse treats that response as information about where you are. The useful thing about information is that it can be true on a day when the answer is nothing at all.
studies.explainEasier: Believers are people whose hearts move when God is named. When his words are read to them, their trust grows stronger. They lean on their Lord for everything.

studies.title: What Makes Belief Real
studies.meaning: A description running since the surah's second ayah ends with two ordinary practices. They stand in prayer, and they give out of what has been provided. Nothing dramatic is named and no quantity is set. The verdict that follows is unusually strong. It calls these the believers in truth, and it lists three things they receive rather than one. Then the passage turns without warning to a march out from home. In the same breath it concedes that a group of the believers did not want to go.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, at the opening of a surah about the encounter at Badr and what came after. The expedition began as an attempt to stop a returning caravan. It became a clash with a much larger armed force sent out to protect it. Some of the believers held back once it was clear what they faced. The early scholars report that plainly. The passage records it rather than smoothing it away.

keyTerms.note: The verb for making something stand and holding it upright, used of a building or a leaning pole. Prayer is not described as performed but as maintained, which shifts the emphasis onto continuity.
Placed after the noun as an intensifier, it works like a stamp of certification on the description. It is not a comparison with other believers but a confirmation that the label actually applies.
An emphatic participle: not merely reluctant but marked as such by the grammar. Placing it inside the same sentence as the departure keeps the account honest about how that morning actually began.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Marching out of Medina meant crossing about eighty miles of open country with little water. The party had few mounts, and men took turns riding. Nobody had set out expecting a battle. The plan was about goods, not fighting. Learning on the road that an armed force was coming to meet them changed the sums entirely. And every man had a household waiting behind him.
studies.didYouKnow: The sentence calling these the believers in truth occurs twice in the Quran. Both times are in this surah, here and again at 8:74. The first time the description behind it is prayer and spending. The second time it is emigration, struggle and the giving of shelter. Both times forgiveness and a generous provision follow.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets the definition of a believer at a level anyone can reach. Neither prayer nor giving is heroic, and neither is given a figure. What follows makes the point sharper. The same people who meet that description are at once shown as reluctant. Belief is defined by what is kept up rather than by what is felt. That is exactly why the reluctance disqualifies nobody.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same verdict at the close of the surah, with a different set of actions behind it.
Opens another passage with the same two practices, prayer and giving, as the marks of belief.
States the principle behind the concession here, that you may dislike what is good for you.

studies.applyIt: Look at your prayer this week not as five separate moments but as a structure you are keeping upright. Which one of them is the pole that keeps slipping? Name it, then decide the single practical change that would hold it: an alarm, a place, a person who prays it beside you. Nothing more ambitious than that.
studies.explainEasier: Real believers keep up their prayer and give from what God has given them. They get a high place with their Lord, forgiveness, and good provision. The verse also says some of them did not want to march out.

studies.title: The One Without Thorns
studies.meaning: Two things are described and neither is denounced. Some argued after the matter had been settled, and the comparison offered for their state is precise: people being driven towards death with their eyes open. Then the choice they had hoped for is named. Two Meccan groups were possible, a loaded caravan and an armed column, and the wish had been for the one carrying no weapons. The passage says plainly that the divine intention ran the other way, towards settling a question rather than towards an easy gain.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, describing the days before the encounter at Badr. A trading caravan returning from Syria was the original target. When it slipped past, an armed force out of Mecca went on towards the wells at Badr anyway. The early scholars report that some of the men argued for turning back. The argument carried on after the decision was made. The passage keeps the disagreement in the record rather than editing it out.

keyTerms.note: A verb form implying argument passing back and forth between two sides rather than a question asked once. Its root carries the sense of twisting a rope tight, so the picture is of a contested pull.

The verb used for driving livestock forward from behind. Applied to men going into battle it keeps their reluctance vivid, while the clause about looking on rules out any suggestion that they misunderstood.
The ordinary word for a thorn, extended in Arabic to weapons and to fighting strength. The caravan is identified as the group without thorns, which is why the wish had settled on it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The caravan trade between Mecca and Syria moved goods worth years of ordinary income. A large returning caravan carried leather, raisins and silver. Taking one outright was a known kind of operation with known rules. That is what the men had come out for. What arrived instead was a body of armed men from their own city. Among them were cousins and brothers. That is a different matter altogether.
studies.didYouKnow: The word the ayah uses for the armed group is the everyday Arabic word for a thorn. This is its only occurrence anywhere in the Quran. Arabic extends the word to weapons and to fighting strength. So the sentence separates the two Meccan groups the way a hand separates two branches. One can be taken hold of. One cannot.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets two intentions side by side and does not pretend they matched. The men wanted a safe gain; what was intended cost more and settled more. Neither is described dishonestly, and the human preference is not called shameful. What the passage establishes is that a desire can be entirely reasonable and still not be what is happening, and that the gap between them proves nothing has gone wrong.

crossReferences.why: States the general form of what happens here: disliking what is good for you, wanting what is not.
Describes the same day from another angle, saying the meeting could not have been arranged deliberately.
Reports a similar argument among believers on a later battlefield, and what was in their minds.

studies.applyIt: Think of a plan of yours that was replaced by something harder, and be honest about the version you had wanted. Do not rush to declare the harder one better. Hold both in view for a minute and notice that your preference was reasonable and simply was not what happened. That is the entire content of these two ayat.
studies.explainEasier: God had promised the men one of two Meccan groups. They hoped for the caravan, because it carried no weapons. What they met was the armed force instead. God meant to settle the matter, not to hand them an easy win.

studies.title: The Cry And The Answer
studies.meaning: The purpose named in the previous ayah is restated in the barest form. One verb for each side: to make the true stand and the false collapse. Then the passage moves back to the night before. The register changes completely, from strategy to a cry for help. The verb chosen is the one used for calling out in extremity. It is not the ordinary verb for asking. What comes back is a number. Early scholars differ over how it relates to the larger figures given elsewhere.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Before the fighting at Badr, the classical sources report that the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) stood praying through the night. He called on God with unusual intensity. This reassurance came in answer. The community was outnumbered by roughly three to one and poorly equipped. They had a small number of mounts between them. Several early collections carry the report of that night in closely similar words.

keyTerms.note: A form of the verb for calling in extremity, from a root also connected with rain that arrives after drought. It is not the ordinary verb for asking, and it assumes the caller is already past managing alone.
From a root meaning to stretch or extend, the same one behind the word for a tide coming in. Help is pictured as a line being lengthened rather than as a rescue arriving out of nowhere.
From the verb for riding behind someone on the same mount. Commentators read it as rank behind rank or as one group following another, and record both readings without deciding between them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Calling for help was a formal act in Arabia with its own vocabulary. A man under attack could shout the name of his clan, and the call placed an obligation on them; failing to answer was a disgrace remembered for years. Everyone present knew what it was to call out for people who might or might not come. On that night the whole reflex was pointed in one direction.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing the angels here occurs only in this ayah in the whole Quran. The early scholars are divided over what it means. Some read rank behind rank, others group following group. The Quran names other numbers for this kind of help as well. Three thousand and then five thousand appear at 3:124 and 3:125. The classical discussion of how the passages fit together is long.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The answer given is not the removal of the danger. The men still fought, and the surah goes on to say that what they saw was made to look manageable rather than made safe. What the reply supplies is company. That distinction runs right through the Quran's treatment of prayer, where the response to a cry is more often presence than rescue, and the ayah that follows says so outright.

crossReferences.why: Says immediately what the reinforcement was actually for, and where help really comes from.
Gives the other numbers of angels, and the same explanation that it was reassurance.
States the general principle of which this night is one particular and very pressed instance.

studies.applyIt: Recall the last time you prayed with real urgency, not the tidy kind. Notice what actually changed afterwards. Often it is not the situation but your capacity to stand inside it. Tonight ask for one specific thing in plain language, then pay attention over the following week to what arrives rather than to what you requested.
studies.explainEasier: The point was to show what is true and to end what is false. On that night the men called out to God for help. He answered and told them he was sending a thousand angels, one after another.

studies.title: Made Only For The Heart
studies.meaning: The ayah narrows twice inside a single line. Arabic's strongest way of limiting a statement is to negate and then allow one exception, and this sentence does it in both halves. What the reinforcement was: nothing except good news and a settling of hearts. Where help comes from: nowhere except God. The two names that close the ayah then answer the question this raises. Strength explains why no instrument is needed; wisdom explains why one was nonetheless provided.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from the account of Badr that fills the first half of this surah. The community was outnumbered. They had come out expecting to intercept goods rather than to fight. The early scholars place this ayah as a comment on the promise of angelic help in the line before. They read it as heading off a conclusion the men would otherwise have drawn from that promise.

keyTerms.note: From a root connected with the skin, since news shows in the face before it reaches speech. The word names the effect a message has on a person rather than the content the message carries.
The verb for something reaching a settled stop, used of ground that levels out and of a bird folding its wings. It describes stillness arrived at after motion, not calm that was there all along.

A single word covers the helping and the winning, so Arabic does not separate the aid from its result. Made definite and placed under a restriction, it says that everything the word covers has one source.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Morale in a small force was everything, and commanders in Arabia knew it. Numbers were shouted. Allies were exaggerated. War poetry was recited to steady men in the hours before contact. The men at Badr had spent the night inside exactly that atmosphere. This ayah takes a piece of encouragement of precisely that kind and says openly what it was for. That is unusual in any account of a battle.
studies.didYouKnow: The pair of names that closes this ayah is the Mighty and the Wise. The pair occurs thirteen times in the Quran. Four of those are in this surah alone, at 8:10, 8:49, 8:63 and 8:67. Each of the four sits at the end of a passage where an outcome has just been taken out of human hands.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah separates a cause from a comfort. The angels are described as doing something to the men, not to the enemy. So the account of the day holds an inward event as well as a military one. It also guards a reader against a common error. The error is simple. It treats the visible means by which help arrived as the reason it arrived at all.

crossReferences.why: Describes the other half of the same reinforcement, what the angels were told to do.
Names the sending down of tranquillity into hearts as its own kind of divine action.
Shows numbers failing on a later day, then the same settling sent down to steady people.

studies.applyIt: Think of a time help arrived through an obvious channel: a person, a phone call, a job. Notice how quickly you filed the channel as the reason. Spend a minute today separating the two, without denying the channel any credit. The habit this ayah is building is not suspicion of means but accuracy about where they sit.
studies.explainEasier: God says the angels were sent as good news, to calm the hearts of the men. Real help comes only from God. He is strong, and he knows what he is doing.

studies.title: Sleep, Water And Firm Ground
studies.meaning: Four things arrive in one sentence, and only the first two are physical. Drowsiness comes over the men and is called a security. That inverts what sleep means on the eve of a fight. Then water falls, and four purposes are listed for it. It washes them. It takes away a defilement attributed to Satan. It binds something over their hearts. It makes their feet firm. Early scholars read the last as real ground and as steady nerve at once, and decline to choose.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, the night before the fighting at Badr. The classical accounts describe the smaller force camped on loose sand near the wells while the larger one held better ground, and report rain falling that night. The passage lists what the weather did and narrates none of the battle. The commentators treat the physical details as reported facts and read the inward effects alongside them rather than in place of them.

keyTerms.note: The verb for draping something across a surface, used of a cloth laid over an object. Sleep is described as arriving from outside and settling on the men rather than as rising up within them.
A noun from the root for safety and trust. Naming drowsiness a security inverts the ordinary reading, since losing alertness before a fight is normally the danger rather than the relief.

keyTerms.gloss: and so that He may bind
keyTerms.note: The verb for tying something fast, used of tethering an animal. Binding upon the heart is an idiom for holding a person together under strain, and the same root names the tethering of horses at 8:60.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Water decided everything in that country. The wells at Badr were the reason both forces were there at all, and whoever held them held the encounter. Sand that has been rained on packs down and carries weight, while dry sand swallows a foot at every step. Men who had walked to the site knew that difference in their legs before anybody explained it to them.
studies.didYouKnow: The classical accounts of the day report that the same rain did opposite things to the two forces, firming the loose sand where the smaller one stood and turning the ground under the larger one heavy. The ayah narrates none of that. It lists four purposes for the water, three of them inward, and leaves the tactics to the historians.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah pairs an inward gift with an outward one and refuses to rank them. Sleep and rain both arrive from outside the person, both are named as acts of God, and both are given plainly practical descriptions. That declines the division between spiritual help and material help. It also treats the body's condition as part of the account, since firm feet and a steadied heart appear in one series with one source.

crossReferences.why: Reports the same experience of sleep coming over a force, in nearly identical wording, on a later day.
Gives the ordinary use of rain sent down for cleansing and for reviving dead land.
Uses the same root for tethering later in the surah, applied there to horses rather than hearts.

studies.applyIt: Notice, for one day, how much of your steadiness is physical. Sleep, water, food, solid ground underfoot. When something frightening is coming, the first honest question is often whether you have slept. This ayah puts drowsiness and rain in the same list as a heart being held together. It offers no apology for that.
studies.explainEasier: God made sleep come over the men that night so they would feel safe. He also sent rain from the sky. It washed them, made their hearts strong, and made the sand under their feet firm.

studies.title: I Am With You
studies.meaning: The instruction is given to angels rather than to men. That is the first thing to register. It opens with a statement of company, not with an order. What the angels are told to do for the believers is to make them firm. That is an inward act. What is said about the other side is inward too: dread placed in hearts. Only then come the two clauses about striking. The classical scholars read those as still addressed to the angels, in that one engagement.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, describing the encounter at Badr. The classical sources connect the ayah to reports of angelic presence at that battle. It sits in a passage that recounts the day from several angles at once. The early scholars are careful about who is addressed. They read the verbs as still aimed at the angels, not at the human force. The surah gives its instructions to people separately, a few ayat later.

keyTerms.note: The verb for fixing something so it cannot shift, used of a peg driven into ground. The angels' first assignment is described as steadying people rather than as fighting on their behalf.

A word for fear that seizes all at once and fills a person, distinct from ordinary apprehension. The Quran attributes it directly to God several times, always as something placed in hearts rather than produced by events.
The plural of the word for a neck. Arabic uses it in idioms for submission and for leadership, but the phrase here is a plainly physical battlefield description belonging to one specific day.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Fighting in that world was close, brief and personal. Lines met within a few paces and men recognised the faces opposite them, since both sides came from the same handful of towns. A battle was usually decided less by casualties than by the moment one side's nerve broke and it turned. That is why an account of the day spends more words on hearts than on weapons.
studies.didYouKnow: Every time the Quran uses this particular word for dread, it attributes it to God rather than to circumstances. That holds in this ayah and in a small number of others about later engagements. The grammar is the same across all of them. The fear is cast or thrown into hearts. The verbs are verbs of placing, never verbs of causing or of frightening.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage describes a battle largely as an event inside people. Believers are steadied and opponents filled with dread. Both are attributed to God, not to anything either force did. That does not make the fighting unreal. It puts the decisive factor somewhere the men could not inspect. The passage also places the angels under instruction. So they stay creatures carrying out an order, not powers of their own.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word for dread cast into hearts, in the account of a different engagement.
Explains what the angelic presence was for, immediately before this description of what it did.
Names the opposite gift, tranquillity sent down on people, in a later account of a hard day.

studies.applyIt: The first thing the angels are told to do is steady people. Do that for someone this week. Not advice and not a solution: presence, and a sentence that says you are not going anywhere. Most people facing something hard need their nerve held more than their problem solved, and the difference usually shows within a minute.
studies.explainEasier: God told the angels that he was with them. He told them to hold the believers steady, and said he would put fear in the hearts of the other side. Then he told them how to strike.

studies.title: Standing On The Other Side
studies.meaning: A reason is supplied for what has just been described. The word chosen for opposition is spatial: to take up the far side of a line. The general rule is then stated, so the particular case becomes one instance of it. The third ayah changes addressee entirely. It speaks to the believers about a battlefield. What it asks for is holding the line while two forces advance towards each other. The passage is describing what held that community together under pressure.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, within the account of Badr. The instruction in the third ayah belongs to a particular kind of engagement. Lines closed on open ground, and one man turning could unravel a whole formation. The early scholars discuss at length whether the instruction was tied to that day or wider. They record the discussion rather than settling it. The ayah right after names two exceptions to it.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning a side or a half. Opposition is described as placing yourself on the other side of a line, which makes the word about position rather than about the temperature of a feeling.

The verb for tasting, used across the Quran of punishment. It converts something abstract into something that reaches a person directly, and it implies first-hand knowledge rather than being told about it.
A word for creeping or crawling forward, used of a large body of men moving as one. It names the interval before contact, when both sides are visible and closing and nobody has struck yet.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A tribal fighting line held only as long as each man trusted the men beside him to stay. There were no ranks and no officers. There was no penalty a commander could impose afterwards. What kept a line together was one certainty. Anyone who ran would be named in poetry for the rest of his life. His family would carry the name after him.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the mass advance in the third ayah occurs only here in the Quran, and it is a word for slow creeping movement rather than a charge. Arabic uses it of a large body shifting forward together, which is what a seventh-century line actually did. Nothing in the passage describes speed.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage gives a reason before it gives an instruction. That is this surah's habit throughout. Naming opposition in spatial terms, as taking the far side of a line, keeps the account off motives nobody can inspect. Placing the address to the believers straight after makes a further point. Both sides of the conflict are measured by one standard, not by two.

crossReferences.why: Names the two exceptions to the instruction given here, in the very next ayah.
Gives the positive form of the same instruction: stand firm, and remember God much.
Uses the identical clause about opposing God and the Messenger, in a quite different setting.

studies.applyIt: Think about the last time you left a difficult situation early: a conversation, a commitment, a room. Not to judge it, but to notice which it was. Repositioning, regrouping, or simply going. The passage takes the first two seriously enough to name them a line later. Being honest about which one you did is the work here.
studies.explainEasier: These people had set themselves against God and his Messenger. The verse says they will be punished for it. It then tells the believers not to run away when they meet an enemy force in the field.

studies.title: Except To Turn And Fight
studies.meaning: A hard sentence with two doors cut into it. Whoever turns his back on that day is described as coming home carrying anger from God. Then two exceptions are named, and they change how the whole thing reads. Turning aside for the fight is one. Moving to join another group is the other. Both are movements away that are not flight. Early scholars disagree over whether the statement applies to that day alone or beyond it. They hold the disagreement in the open rather than resolving it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following directly from the previous ayah and belonging to the account of Badr. The phrase naming that day is what the disagreement turns on. Some early scholars read it as limiting the statement to the battle in question; others as a way of saying any day of that kind. Both readings are old, and the classical commentaries record them side by side without treating either as settled.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning an edge or a side. It describes moving off the straight line for a purpose, which is why this movement is separated from flight by intention rather than by direction.
From the root for occupying a space. It names moving towards where other people are, so a man who leaves alone and a man who leaves to reach his own side are not doing the same thing.

The verb for returning home with something in hand. It makes the anger a thing brought back rather than a sentence pronounced, which is how the Quran generally describes what people bring upon themselves.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian fighting was fluid. Small groups broke off, circled, regrouped and re-entered, and the distance between a manoeuvre and a rout could be a few seconds and a man's intention. Everyone watching believed they could tell the difference, and everyone could be wrong. The exceptions in this ayah are written by someone who knew what a battlefield actually looks like from inside it.
studies.didYouKnow: Both words naming the exceptions occur only in this ayah and nowhere else in the Quran. They are technical, drawn from the vocabulary of movement in a fight: one from the root for an edge or flank, the other from the root for taking up a space. Neither has any moral colour of its own.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The severity and the exceptions belong together. Without the exceptions, every tactical movement would have been a moral failure. Without the severity, every frightened man would have had a cover story. What the ayah shows is that one physical act can be two entirely different things. The difference lies in a purpose. Only the person and God can actually see it.

crossReferences.why: States the instruction that this ayah immediately qualifies with two named exceptions.
Describes people who did turn away on a later day, and what is said about them afterwards.
Addresses the calculation behind flight rather than its conditions, during a later siege.

studies.applyIt: There is a difference between stepping back to think and walking out. You know which one you have been doing with a particular problem. Name it accurately to yourself today, in one sentence. Do not decide anything else yet. The two exceptions are in this ayah because the difference is real and cannot be seen from outside.
studies.explainEasier: Anyone who ran away that day would carry God's anger. But there were two exceptions. A man could turn to attack from another side, or move to join up with his own group.

studies.title: You Did Not Throw
studies.meaning: A victory is described by taking it away from the people who won it. Then the sentence does something stranger still. It denies an act and affirms it in one breath: you did not throw when you threw. The classical scholars read this as separating the motion from its effect. The man is granted the movement; the outcome is withheld. The stated purpose then arrives as a testing of the believers by something good. That makes the victory itself the trial rather than its reward.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical sources connect the second clause to a reported moment at Badr. The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) took a handful of dust or gravel from the ground and threw it towards the opposing line. Several early collections carry the report. The early scholars treat it as the occasion of the phrase. The wider denial about the killing is read as covering the whole engagement.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary verb for throwing or shooting. Its appearance three times in one short clause, first denied, then affirmed, then reassigned, is what makes the sentence famous among commentators on Arabic style.
The noun ordinarily means an affliction, and pairing it with the adjective for what is beautiful is deliberate. It says that being handed a victory is itself a form of being tested.
An active participle from the root for feebleness. What is described as weakened is not the men opposite but their planning, so the claim concerns a scheme losing its force rather than casualties.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Badr was fought on sand between low rises, and dust was the one thing that ground offered without limit. At close quarters, wind-carried grit in the eyes was a genuine nuisance and everyone had experienced it. A handful of it thrown towards a line could not injure anybody, and nobody present would have thought otherwise. That ordinary fact is what makes the sentence about the throw so pointed.
studies.didYouKnow: The short clause in the middle of this ayah uses one verb three times in a row. It is denied, then affirmed, then reassigned to God. Arabic grammarians and early scholars have written a great deal about this. A single act is negated and confirmed inside one sentence. The usual explanation separates the motion, which was a man's, from the effect, which was not.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage does not say that human action is unreal. The throw happened. The fighting happened. The men are addressed throughout as the ones who did it. What is denied is the weight people naturally give their own effort as a cause. That leaves human action fully required and fully insufficient at once. The Quran keeps returning to this position whenever effort and outcome are discussed together.

crossReferences.why: States the same relation between a human act and its maker, well away from any battlefield.
Makes the parallel statement about victory, that it comes from God and nowhere else.
Describes another part of the same day, where even what people saw was arranged.

studies.applyIt: Think of one thing you did well recently and describe it twice: once as your own effort, honestly and without false modesty, and once as a set of conditions you did not arrange, such as health, timing, or the person who mentioned your name. Both accounts are true. This ayah holds them in one sentence, and so can you.
studies.explainEasier: The verse tells the men that they did not really kill their enemies. God did. And when the Prophet threw dust at them, it was God who threw it, not him.

studies.title: The Verdict You Asked For
studies.meaning: The address turns to the other side and answers a request they had made. They asked for a decision; the passage tells them one has been delivered. Then two conditional sentences run in parallel: stop and it is better for you, come back and so will We. Offer and warning are given in the same grammatical shape, which sets them on equal footing. The closing clause explains why numbers will not help, and it is not a claim about relative strength.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical sources report that before the fighting at Badr one of the Meccan leaders prayed publicly at the Sacred House for God to decide between the two parties and destroy whichever was more in the wrong. The commentators connect this ayah to that request. The verb used for asking is built on the root for opening, which Arabic also uses for asking a judge to open a case.

keyTerms.note: From the root for opening. Arabic uses this form for asking a judge to open a case and hand down a ruling, so the request was for the matter to be settled rather than for help in winning.
The same root as the verb just before it, which is why the reply lands as it does. The word later becomes the ordinary Arabic term for a conquest, and names a whole surah.
A word for a group that stands together, used throughout this surah of both sides. Saying it will not avail however numerous makes the point about relation rather than about size.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Oaths and appeals made at the Sacred House carried weight across the Hijaz, whatever a listener believed. A man who called publicly on God to judge between two parties was staking his standing on the answer, and the audience remembered such words and repeated them afterwards. Asking for a verdict in that setting was not a private prayer. It was a public wager with witnesses.
studies.didYouKnow: The root behind both the request and the reply here means to open. It later names surah 48. There the same word describes a settlement reached without a battle. The Quran uses this root for opening a door, for opening a case for judgement, and for opening a city. It lets the three senses run into one another rather than keeping them apart.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage takes a request seriously and answers it, which is the striking part. A prayer made against the believers is treated as a genuine prayer and given a genuine reply. It also holds the door open in the same breath as it warns, and the offer comes first in the sentence. That ordering, desist before return, is how this surah handles its opponents throughout.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same offer to the same audience: desist, and what is past will be forgiven.
Records another prayer made by the same side, asking for stones to fall from the sky.
Uses the same verb for seeking a decision, applied there to an earlier community.

studies.applyIt: Be careful about the arguments you ask to have settled. Most of us pray to be proved right without quite meaning it literally. Pick one dispute you have wanted a verdict on, and ask honestly whether you would accept the answer if it went the other way. If not, you were asking for something else.
studies.explainEasier: One side had asked God to judge between them. The verse tells them the judgement has now come. If they stop, that is better for them. If they come back, God will meet them again.

studies.title: Hearing Without Hearing
studies.meaning: Three ayat turning on a single verb. The first asks for obedience and adds a clause that makes turning away worse: while you are hearing. The second names people who said the right sentence and did not do what it describes, so the saying is itself the failure. The third delivers a verdict in the harshest terms this surah uses, and the fault it names at the end is not deafness but the refusal to reason. Early scholars note that the deafness described is chosen rather than physical.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, inside the surah's account of the year of Badr. The community was newly assembled, and its instructions travelled by voice, delivered and repeated aloud. The early scholars report no single occasion. They read the passage as addressing those slow to act on what they had been told. The second ayah, they say, addresses opponents who claimed to have listened. The ayat sit between a battle account and an appeal to the community.

keyTerms.note: A present tense describing something still going on. Turning away is faulted not in general but specifically while the words are still arriving, which makes the timing part of what is wrong with it.
The plural of a word for anything that walks the earth, from a verb meaning to creep along. It is deliberately wide, covering animals and people together, and this surah uses the phrase twice.

The verb comes from the word for a tether used to hobble a camel. Reasoning is binding things so they do not wander off, which makes its absence a kind of looseness rather than a shortage of information.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Everything in Medina moved by ear. Announcements were called out, agreements were witnessed by listeners, and poetry was the medium of both argument and record. A man's competence was measured partly by how well he held what he had heard once. In that setting, claiming to have heard and then acting as though you had not was a recognised and shameful kind of failure.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase naming the worst of creatures occurs twice in the Quran, both times in this surah, at 8:22 and again thirty-three ayat later at 8:55. The wording is identical up to the point where the description begins. The first names people who do not reason; the second names people who break every agreement they make.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage locates the failure in reception rather than in access. Everybody in the scene heard the same words. What separates them is what happened after the sound arrived. The closing verb makes that a matter of using the mind, not of holding the right information. The passage also makes a claim about language. Saying that you have understood is named as the very thing that can hide not understanding.

crossReferences.why: Records the same split between the words said and the action taken, in an earlier community.
Extends the picture of working faculties left unused, and arrives at the same verdict.
Shows the kind of hearing that leaves nothing behind, in a later Medinan setting.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing you have heard repeatedly and agreed with and have never acted on. A single specific thing. Do the smallest version of it today, before you hear it said again. The passage is not against listening. It is against the particular comfort of feeling that agreeing is already a kind of doing.
studies.explainEasier: The verse tells believers to obey God and his Messenger. It says not to walk away while the words are still being said. It warns them not to be like people who say they heard when they did not.

studies.title: Hearing Would Not Have Helped
studies.meaning: An imagined case, answered by a second imagined case. The first grants what a sympathetic listener would want. Had there been anything in them to work with, they would have been made to hear. The second closes the door the first opened. Even then, it says, they would have turned away. Early scholars read this as a statement about a settled bent, not about a decree issued in advance. They also note that it follows straight on a description of people who claimed they had heard.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing a passage that has just called claimed hearing a failure. The early scholars tie the ayah to no named individual. They read it as addressing people in and around Medina who engaged with the message in words. Those people showed no intention of acting on it. The ayah answers a question the preceding ayat raise. The question is why such people are not simply given something clearer.

keyTerms.note: Indefinite and unqualified, so it names the smallest quantity of anything usable. What is said to be missing is not merit but material, nothing to build on rather than a poor record.

keyTerms.gloss: He would have made them hear
keyTerms.note: A causative form: not speaking to them but bringing about hearing in them. That places the failure inside the listener, since the sound was already arriving without any difficulty.
From a root meaning a side or a breadth. To turn away is to present your side rather than your face, which describes a posture towards a speaker rather than a judgement about the content.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Public argument in Medina happened in courtyards and at the edges of the market. Anyone could listen. Going to a gathering cost nothing and committed you to nothing. A man could stand at the back of a circle for an hour and hear everything. He could agree with the reasonable parts and walk home unchanged. That was a familiar figure in the city, and the passage is describing him.
studies.didYouKnow: In the four ayat from 8:20 to 8:23 the verb for hearing appears five times. The ayah in the middle of them adds the word for the deaf as well. Nothing else in the passage is repeated at anything like that rate. The repetition is what carries the argument. No plain statement of it is ever made.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah makes a claim that is uncomfortable and precise. It does not say these people were stopped from hearing. It says hearing would not have changed the outcome. The obstacle does not sit in what reaches them. That leaves human responsibility intact while denying that more evidence is the missing piece. It also warns a reader against treating their own understanding as something owned rather than given.

crossReferences.why: Makes the same claim about additional proof, and lists what would still not be enough.
Names the condition this ayah then explains, a deafness that is chosen rather than physical.
Describes the same closure with a different image, and is discussed alongside this ayah by commentators.

studies.applyIt: There is advice you have been given more than once and quietly decided is not for you. Not rejected out loud, just set aside. Take one piece of it this week and act on it for three days without arguing with it in your head. You are not testing the advice. You are testing whether you were ever listening.
studies.explainEasier: The verse says that if there had been any good in these people, God would have made them hear. Even if he had, they would still have turned their backs. They would have walked off.

studies.title: The Call That Gives Life
studies.meaning: The summons is described by its effect. Responding is called being brought to life, which assumes the hearer is not fully alive without it. Then a sentence that stops the passage. God comes between a person and their own heart. Early scholars read that as His power over the inner life, and as a warning that a heart is not securely your own. The second verse widens the frame, since the trial named does not fall only on those who caused it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from the surah dealing with Badr and its aftermath. The community was newly settled. Its internal disagreements were starting to have consequences beyond the people involved. Early scholars read the warning about a trial reaching more than the wrongdoers as addressed to that situation. They preserve reports of early Muslims applying it to conflicts that arose later.

keyTerms.note: A form of the verb to answer that implies compliance rather than mere reply. The same word is used of God answering a supplication, so the human answer is put in the vocabulary usually reserved for His.
A verb for interposing and for change, used of standing between two things to keep them apart. Early scholars preserve its ambiguity, reading both separation and transformation in it.
Originally the assaying of gold by fire to separate it from what is mixed in. The word covers testing and the civil strife that tests a community, and both senses are active in this warning.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Tribal conflict spread by design. A dispute between two men obliged their clans, and allies were drawn in by prior oaths, so a quarrel that began at a well could end with settlements burned. Nobody in that world imagined a fight staying private. The warning about a trial that does not confine itself to the guilty described a mechanism the audience had watched work all their lives.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause about God coming between a person and their heart is one of the shortest in the Quran to have produced a long tradition of comment. Readings range from His knowledge of what is hidden to His power to turn a heart in a new direction. Classical authorities record the range without settling it. The openness is generally treated as intended.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage denies a comfortable assumption. Whatever else is uncertain, a person at least owns their own inner life. Putting God between someone and their heart removes that last private ground. It does so in the middle of a call to respond, so the urgency is practical. What can be done now may not stay available. The second verse then removes another comfort, that consequences stay with the people who earned them.

crossReferences.why: Describes being brought to life from death and given a light to walk by.
Asks that hearts not be turned aside after guidance, which assumes that they can be.
Applies the warning about discord directly to a community losing its strength.

studies.applyIt: Think of a good intention you have been carrying for months without acting on. Do the first physical step today, however small, before the intention gets any older. The warning here is not about wickedness. It is about the distance that can open between a person and what they meant, and how quietly that happens.
studies.explainEasier: God is calling you to something that will make you truly alive, so answer him. Remember that God stands between a person and his own heart. And trouble in a group does not stay with the guilty only.

studies.title: When You Were Few
studies.meaning: An instruction to remember, and what is to be remembered is specified rather than left general: not hardship in the abstract but a particular fear, of being snatched away. Three verbs then describe the change, and they run in an order. Shelter first, then support, then provision. Early scholars note that the sequence matters, since a group needs somewhere to stand before it can be helped, and helping before it can be fed. The purpose named at the end is thankfulness, not confidence.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Before the emigration the Muslim community in Mecca was small. It was effectively unprotected once the clan arrangements covering it began to fail. The verb used for being snatched fits a real danger in Arabia. A small group without allies could be seized on the road. The early scholars read the ayah as addressed to a community that had already begun to forget how recent that condition was.

keyTerms.note: A passive form: not weak but rendered weak by others. Arabic distinguishes this sharply from ordinary weakness, and the Quran uses it of people whose condition is somebody else's doing.
The verb for grabbing something suddenly and carrying it off, used of a bird taking prey. It conveys speed and helplessness together rather than defeat at the end of a struggle.

The verb for taking someone in and housing them. The same root supplies the word used later in this surah for the people of Medina who sheltered the emigrants, which quietly names how the shelter arrived.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Safety in Arabia was a question of who would avenge you. A man travelled under the protection of his clan, and a group with nobody to answer for it could be robbed or seized without consequence. Small communities attached themselves to larger ones for exactly this reason. The fear named in this ayah was not imagined; it was the ordinary arithmetic of the road.
studies.didYouKnow: The two things this ayah credits to God, shelter and support, are named by the same two verbs used later in the surah for the people of Medina, at 8:72 and 8:74, where they are described as those who gave shelter and gave help. The ayah says God did it. The later ayat name the hands it came through.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah asks for memory as a religious act. It specifies the memory rather than leaving it vague. Remembering a condition you are no longer in is hard. The change starts to feel like the natural state. Naming fear, shelter, support and food in that order builds a chain, and each link is credited outward. And the stated purpose is thankfulness rather than security.

crossReferences.why: Asks for the same kind of remembering, of a condition the community had already left behind.
Names the people through whom the shelter described here actually reached the emigrants.
Names the same two gifts, food against hunger and safety from fear, given to another group.

studies.applyIt: Write down in one line something you were genuinely afraid of five years ago that is simply not a feature of your life now. Not necessarily solved by you; just gone. Most people cannot name one without stopping to think, which is the ayah's point exactly. Keep the line somewhere you will come across it again.
studies.explainEasier: God tells them to remember when they were few and weak. They were afraid that people would snatch them away. Then God gave them a safe place, helped them win, and gave them good things to live on.

studies.title: What Was Left In Your Hands
studies.meaning: Two instructions and then a reason. Betrayal is named at three levels inside one sentence. Of God, of the Messenger, and of the trusts held between people. The short clause at the end, while you know, removes the excuse of not having realised. The second ayah then supplies a motive without accusing anyone of holding it. Property and children are named as a trial. That identifies what usually makes a person break faith. And it does so without calling either of them bad.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The early scholars report more than one occasion for the first ayah. Several involve secret information passed to an interested party. They do not settle on one account. The setting was a city where the community's plans were known to a small number of people. Family ties ran straight across the lines of the conflict. Keeping a confidence often meant choosing against your own relatives.

keyTerms.note: The verb for failing something entrusted to you, distinct from stealing and from lying. It requires a prior relationship of confidence, which is why the same root gives the word for a treacherous friend.
From the root for safety and belief. What is entrusted and the faith placed in you share a root in Arabic, so breaking a trust and breaking faith are named by one family of words.
Originally the assaying of metal by fire to separate it from its ore. Calling wealth and children a trial says they reveal what a person is made of, not that they are a punishment or a trap.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Deposits were the banking system of Arabia. A traveller left goods, money or a weapon with a trusted man and collected them on his return, with no document and no court to appeal to. A reputation for returning what was left with you was the most valuable asset a merchant could hold, and losing it ended a career. The ayah's word comes straight out of that practice.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a trust here is built on one root. The people of Mecca used a title from that root for the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). They used it before the revelation began. It means the trustworthy one. The ordinary Arabic words for faith and for safety come from the same root. The vocabulary makes reliability and belief branches of one idea.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage refuses to separate a person's dealings with God from their dealings with people. All three betrayals appear in one sentence, under one verb. The second ayah then does something unusual: it names the pressure honestly instead of demanding that it be absent. Wealth and children are not condemned anywhere in it. They are identified as the place where the test is most likely to fall.

crossReferences.why: States the positive form, handing back what was entrusted, as a standing obligation on everyone.
Repeats the second ayah here almost word for word, including the reward named after it.
Uses the same word for a trust at the largest possible scale, as something offered and carried.

studies.applyIt: Think of one piece of information someone gave you in confidence that would be interesting to repeat. Notice the small pull towards telling it; that pull is the entire subject of these two ayat. Do not repeat it this week. Notice also what you would have gained by repeating it, and how little that turns out to be.
studies.explainEasier: The verse tells believers not to break faith with God or with his Messenger. It also says not to break faith with what people have left in their care. Money and children, it says, are a test.

studies.title: A Criterion To Tell By
studies.meaning: A condition and three results. If you keep awareness of God, you are given a criterion, your bad deeds are covered over, and you are forgiven. Early scholars explain the first as a power to tell things apart, a discernment that comes with practice rather than with study. The order is worth noticing. The gift of telling things apart is named before the wiping away of what is past. So clarity arrives as a consequence, not as a reward for being clear already.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from the surah on Badr. The passage recalls the community's earlier weakness in Mecca and the shelter given to it afterwards. The verse sits between reminders of past danger and warnings about betraying trusts. Early scholars record no specific occasion. They read it as a general promise, placed where the community most needed a way of judging hard situations for itself.

keyTerms.gloss: a criterion, a means of separating
keyTerms.note: From the root for splitting apart. The same word names the day of Badr elsewhere in this surah and is used of revelation, so it covers anything that divides truth from its counterfeit.

From a root meaning to cover, the same one behind the word for a farmer who buries seed. Wrongs are described as covered rather than undone, which early scholars keep distinct from the forgiveness named next.
What exceeds what is owed. Naming it at the end frames all three results as gifts rather than as payments, even though the sentence opened with a condition attached to them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Judging situations without institutions was a daily skill. A merchant weighed a partner's honesty on a handshake. A traveller decided whom to trust on a road. A tribe judged whether a peace offer was genuine. There were no records to consult and no authority to appeal to. Discernment was the practical skill that kept people alive, and a promise of better discernment landed as a promise of safety.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for criterion appears twice in this surah with different references. Once it is something given to a person. Once it names the day of Badr itself, the day of separation. It also titles surah 25, and it is used of revelation elsewhere. So one term names a book, a day and a faculty.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Moral clarity is presented as the fruit of conduct rather than its precondition. That reverses the usual assumption. Normally a person must first know what is right and then act on it. Here, acting with awareness produces the power to tell. The claim is not that God supplies information. It is that the power of telling apart sharpens with use. Forgiveness follows, which keeps the promise from depending on having judged rightly so far.

crossReferences.why: Attaches a similar promise to the same condition, a way out and provision from nowhere.
Ends with the same construction, teaching following from awareness of God.
Uses the same word as the name of the day the two forces met at Badr.

studies.applyIt: Take one decision this week where you are genuinely unsure, and before you weigh the options, do something small you know is right and have been putting off. Then come back to the decision. The verse puts the order that way round, and the claim is testable in a single afternoon.
studies.explainEasier: If you stay careful about God, he will give you a way of telling right from wrong. He will cover over your bad deeds and forgive you. God gives more than anyone is owed.

studies.title: They Planned And So Did He
studies.meaning: A memory addressed to one person. The three options are listed as they were argued: to hold him, to kill him, or to drive him out. Then the sentence turns, and the same verb is used of both sides without softening. Early scholars handle this carefully, since the word for scheming is applied to God. They explain it as answering a hidden plan in kind, not as deceit. The superlative at the close settles the outcome before any of the story is told.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan in what it describes, Medinan in placement. The classical sources report a gathering of Meccan leaders shortly before the emigration at which these three courses were debated, and the ayah addresses the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) directly about it. By the time this surah came, the plot had failed years earlier. It is recalled to make a point about the battle just described.

keyTerms.note: From the same root as making firm, used earlier in this surah of steadying the believers. Here the fixing in place is hostile, so one word covers both being supported and being detained.
The verb for planning that the other party cannot see. Commentators are careful when it is used of God, explaining it as answering a hidden plan in kind rather than as any kind of deception.
The superlative in front of it makes the claim comparative rather than absolute: among those who plan, one plan holds. The same phrase closes an ayah in surah 3 about another prophet.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca had no ruler and no police. Decisions were made by an assembly of clan heads who had to reach something like agreement, because any action against a man would be answered by his own relatives. Killing someone under a clan's protection meant a blood feud with that clan. That constraint is exactly why the meeting described had to weigh three options rather than simply act.
studies.didYouKnow: The sentence that turns here, saying that they planned and God planned and that God is the best of planners, occurs twice in the Quran in almost identical words. The other occurrence is at 3:54, where it describes a plot against a different prophet. Both times the scheme in question is aimed directly at a prophet's life.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage does not deny the plot's seriousness or suggest that it was doomed by its nature. It says that a second plan was running in the same period. That is a different consolation from the one people usually offer, which is that things will work out in the end. What is asserted here is not an outcome but a presence: somebody else was also acting, with more information.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same sentence about scheming answered by scheming, in a plot against another prophet.
Describes the escape that followed the plot named here, seen from inside the journey itself.
States the principle at its largest scale, that no scheme falls outside the reckoning.

studies.applyIt: Recall a time something was being arranged against you that you only learned about later. Notice that through those weeks you carried on, unaware, and were fine. You are almost certainly inside a period like that now. The ayah does not promise you a good outcome. It tells you that you are not the only one acting.
studies.explainEasier: The leaders in Mecca met and planned what to do about him. They wanted to lock him up, kill him, or drive him out. They made their plan, and God made his. God is the best planner.

studies.title: Tales Of The Ancients
studies.meaning: A claim in three parts, and only the middle one is a boast. They say they have heard, which concedes the reception. They say they could produce the like of it if they chose, which is a claim never acted on. And they file what they heard under old stories, which is the move that lets them stop thinking about it. Early scholars note that the second and third claims undercut each other, since what needs only a decision is not the same as what is merely inherited.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan in placement, describing an attitude formed in Mecca. The Quran issues a challenge in several surahs, to produce anything like it. This ayah reports the response of people who had heard that challenge. They answered with a statement of intent rather than an attempt. The dismissive phrase they reach for turns up again and again across the Quran. It is nearly always in the mouths of the same kind of speaker.

keyTerms.note: A conditional that costs nothing to utter. Arabic marks this construction as contrary to fact, so the grammar itself concedes that the wishing did not happen and the producing was never attempted.
From a root meaning lines written in rows. The word carries no charge of falsehood on its own; what makes the phrase dismissive is the second half, which files the material under a closed past.

The plural of the word for first. Attaching it to stories makes the objection chronological rather than substantive: not that the content is wrong, but that it belongs to people already finished with.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca had professional storytellers, and traders came back from Syria and Iraq carrying tales with them. Accounts of vanished peoples and ruined cities filled long evenings. Everyone had heard several versions. Filing a new recitation under that heading was the quickest way to make it harmless. It moved the words from something that needed an answer to something that needed only an audience.
studies.didYouKnow: The dismissal used here calls the recitation tales of the ancients. It appears nine times in the Quran, across both Meccan and Medinan surahs. It is nearly always in the mouths of objectors. It nearly always follows a description of them hearing the ayat recited. The Quran quotes the objection far more often than it stops to answer it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage records a refusal that is not an argument. Nothing in the reported speech engages with what was said. The claim to be able to match it is never tested. The label applied to it does nothing except close the file. That is an accurate description of how people usually decline something. Putting it in the text lets a reader recognise the move when they make it themselves.

crossReferences.why: States the challenge this boast claims it could meet, and predicts that it will not be attempted.
Answers the boast at its largest scale, naming who would have to combine and what would follow.
Reports the identical phrase about tales of the ancients from the same kind of listener.

studies.applyIt: Notice the label you reach for when something asks more of you than you want to give. Old-fashioned. Obvious. Not for me. Heard it before. Pick one thing you have filed that way and unfile it for a week. You do not have to accept it. Just stop letting the label do your thinking for you.
studies.explainEasier: When God's verses were read to them, they said they had heard it all before. They claimed they could write the same thing if they wanted to. Then they called it old stories from long ago.

studies.title: Two Reasons It Did Not Fall
studies.meaning: A prayer is quoted, and it is a strange one: asking for punishment rather than for proof, on the condition that the message is true. The reply then gives two reasons the request was not granted, and neither concerns the merit of the people asking. The first is a presence among them. The second is that forgiveness was still being sought there. Early scholars differ over who is described as seeking it, some reading believers still in Mecca and others the speakers themselves.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan in placement, reporting words spoken in Mecca. The classical sources connect the prayer to a challenge issued in public. They record more than one account of who said it. The ayah answering it belongs to a passage with a larger question in view. That question is why the Meccan opposition had not simply been destroyed, after everything the surah has just described about Badr.

keyTerms.note: A special vocative form, marked with a suffix rather than the usual particle in front. It occurs only five times in the Quran and carries a formality ordinary address does not, which makes the request more deliberate.

The causative of the verb for rain. The Quran generally reaches for this form when what falls is destructive, and for different verbs when rain arrives as a mercy, so the choice already carries the disaster.
The verb for asking to be covered over, from a root that also gives the word for a helmet. Commentators divide over who is meant here and record the readings without preferring one of them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Calling down disaster on yourself to prove a point was a known move in Arabia. It worked because everyone believed such calls could be answered. Oaths of self-cursing were sworn at shrines and taken seriously by both parties. The men who said these words were making a public wager that nothing would happen. They staked their standing on the silence that followed.
studies.didYouKnow: The form used here to address God occurs only five times in the whole Quran. One opens a prayer about sovereignty. One asks for a table of food to be sent down. One is spoken by the people of the Garden. One opens an appeal for judgement. And this one asks for punishment to fall. It is the same form used at the start of many supplications today.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reply is remarkable for what it declines to say. It does not defend the people asking. It does not deny that they deserved what they requested. It points to no good in them. It names two outside circumstances instead: a presence, and a practice still going on in the city. Restraint is presented as resting on things happening in a place, not on a verdict about the people there.

crossReferences.why: Gives another reason a demanded sign was withheld, resting on the same kind of restraint.
Reports the same demand for punishment to be brought forward, and the answer given to it.
Continues immediately from here, taking up the question of why they would be punished at all.

studies.applyIt: There is a version of this prayer that people make quietly: if this is right, prove it by ruining me. It sounds like courage and is usually exhaustion. If you have said something like it recently, notice that the reply here contains no verdict on the speaker at all. Ask instead, plainly, for the thing you actually want.
studies.explainEasier: Some people asked God to drop stones on them from the sky if the message was true. God did not punish them. The verse gives two reasons. The Prophet was still among them. And people there were still asking for forgiveness.

studies.title: Whistling At The House
studies.meaning: A question is put, and the answer redefines who counts as a guardian. The people controlling access to the Sacred House are said not to be its guardians. The qualification offered in place of theirs is not lineage or ownership. It is mindfulness of God. Their worship at the site is then described in two words that belong to no religious vocabulary. Whistling and clapping. Early scholars explain these as real noises made there. They note that the ayah reports the sound and no content at all.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan in placement, describing Mecca. Access to the Sacred House, and the offices attached to it, were held by particular families. They carried standing and income with them. Pilgrims came from across Arabia, and those who managed the site benefited. The early scholars report that in the years before the emigration Muslims were kept from praying there. That is the barring this ayah names.

keyTerms.note: The verb for blocking or diverting somebody from a path. Its object here is people rather than the message, so what is described is physical prevention rather than argument against a claim.

From a root meaning nearness. The word covers custodian, ally and protector together, so the ayah denies a relationship rather than only an office, and substitutes a moral qualification for an inherited one.
Two words that occur only here in the Quran. Commentators explain them as noises made at the House, and the criticism lies in the reporting: sound is named, and nothing else is.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The Sacred House stood at the centre of an economy as well as of worship. Pilgrimage brought traders, and the families holding the keys, the water rights and the right to feed pilgrims drew standing from it every year. Being told they were not the guardians of the House was not a remark about piety. It was a claim about who the place belonged with, and it touched money.
studies.didYouKnow: Both words describing the worship at the House occur only in this ayah and nowhere else in the Quran. The classical scholars had to work out their meanings from old poetry and from reports about practice at the site. They broadly agree that one names a whistling sound and the other a clapping. They differ over the details of each.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates custody from qualification. Holding the keys is described as not amounting to guardianship. What replaces it is a quality rather than a credential. That claim reaches a long way. It applies to anyone running a sacred place anywhere. The passage also treats worship as having content. The criticism is not that the noise was wrong. It is that noise was the whole of it.

crossReferences.why: Names the same offence, keeping people from a place of prayer, as a form of injustice.
Sets custodianship of the House against the qualification for it, as a direct question.
Repeats the pairing of barring people and the Sacred House, in a passage about pilgrimage.

studies.applyIt: Think of a place you hold a formal role in: a family, a workplace, a mosque committee. Ask what you would still be qualified for if the role were taken away tomorrow. The criterion in this ayah is not the title. Spend ten minutes this week on the part of that job nobody would notice if you stopped doing it.
studies.explainEasier: These people kept others away from the Sacred House, but it was not really theirs to guard. Those who are careful about God are its true guardians. Their own worship there was just whistling and clapping.

studies.title: Money Spent Into Regret
studies.meaning: A sequence in four steps, and the passage lets it run without comment. They spend. The spending continues. It turns into a grief for them. Then they are overcome. What makes it striking is that the money never achieves anything at any stage. Barring people is the intention, not the result. Early scholars connect the ayah to funds raised for a further campaign. They read the word for grief as the ache of an expense that bought nothing.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical sources report that after the reverse at Badr, money was collected in Mecca to pay for another campaign. The early scholars connect this ayah to that effort. Some tie it more narrowly to a caravan whose profits were set aside for the purpose. The reports agree on the general situation, a war paid for out of private wealth. They differ on the particulars.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary Quranic verb for spending in a cause, used everywhere else of giving in God's way. Leaving the word unmodified here makes the contrast structural: an identical action pointed in the opposite direction.
From a root meaning to strip something bare or to exhaust an animal. It names the particular ache of realising that effort went for nothing, which is why it suits money better than defeat.
